chief_complaint: newborn male infant with unilateral complete cleft lip and palate requiring multidisciplinary staging and repair
hpi_details: 2-week-old male infant brought by parents for initial plastic surgery cleft clinic evaluation. Born at term with congenital left unilateral complete cleft lip extending into the left nostril floor associated with a complete cleft of the hard and soft palate. Parents report significant feeding difficulties with nasal regurgitation of formula when using standard bottles.
ideas: parents overwhelmed and grieving the facial difference, feeling anxious about multiple surgeries
concerns: parents terrified baby is not getting enough nutrition due to milk coming out of his nose
expectations: want clear explanation of the surgical timeline from babyhood to adulthood and immediate feeding guidance
pmh: Born 39 weeks normal vaginal delivery, birth weight 3.4 kg, current weight 3.3 kg

clinical_knowledge.topic: Congenital Left Unilateral Complete Cleft Lip and Palate without syndromic features evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Congenital Left Unilateral Complete Cleft Lip and Palate without syndromic features is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes multidisciplinary cleft team care with feeding optimization and pre-surgical nasoalveolar molding prior to staged repair, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: newborn male infant with unilateral complete cleft lip and palate requiring multidisciplinary staging and repair

Key HPI features: 2-week-old male infant brought by parents for initial plastic surgery cleft clinic evaluation. Born at term with congenital left unilateral complete cleft lip extending into the left nostril floor associated with a complete cleft of the hard and soft palate. Parents report significant feeding difficulties with nasal regurgitation of formula when using standard bottles.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 140, RR 36, Weight 3.3 kg. Facial exam demonstrates complete left-sided cleft lip disrupting the vermilion, white roll, Cupid's bow, and floor of the nose with significant splaying and flattening of the left alar cartilage and nasal asymmetry. Intraoral examination confirms wide cleft involving the primary and secondary palate through the alveolus, hard palate, and soft palate uvula. Heart and lung exams normal. No syndromic dysmorphic features.
Relevant background/PMH: Born 39 weeks normal vaginal delivery, birth weight 3.4 kg, current weight 3.3 kg
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Congenital Left Unilateral Complete Cleft Lip and Palate without syndromic features.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Soft tissue infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Flap ischemia or tissue necrosis.
management_principles: Multidisciplinary Cleft Team care: optimize feeding and prepare the alveolar/nasal anatomy for staged surgical repair.
Feeding optimization immediately: prescribe specialized Haberman feeder or Mead-Johnson squeeze bottle with upright feeding posture; consult pediatric speech/feeding therapist
Pre-surgical infant orthopedics: initiate Nasoalveolar Molding (NAM) appliance to approximate alveolar segments and mold nasal cartilage prior to surgery
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 2-week-old male presenting with congenital unilateral complete cleft lip and palate and secondary feeding difficulties.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 140, RR 36, Weight 3.3 kg. Facial exam demonstrates complete left-sided cleft lip disrupting the vermilion, white roll, Cupid's bow, and floor of the nose with significant splaying and flattening of the left alar cartilage and nasal asymmetry. Intraoral examination confirms wide cleft involving the primary and secondary palate through the alveolus, hard palate, and soft palate uvula. Heart and lung exams normal. No syndromic dysmorphic features.
reference_soap.assessment: Congenital Left Unilateral Complete Cleft Lip and Palate without syndromic features.
reference_soap.plan: Multidisciplinary cleft-team care: promptly assess feeding safety, hydration, weight gain, hearing, and associated anomalies; provide an individualized feeding plan with pediatric feeding support. Discuss nasoalveolar molding and staged lip/palate repair only with the cleft, pediatric, anesthesia, and family teams after the infant is clinically ready; technique and timing must be individualized rather than determined by a fixed rule alone.

learning_objectives: Recognize anatomical components disrupted in unilateral complete cleft lip and palate (lip vermilion, orbicularis oris sphincter, nasal alar cartilage, primary/secondary palate)
Explain the clinical requirements of the 'Rule of Tens' (10 weeks age, 10 pounds weight, 10 g/dL hemoglobin) prior to primary cleft lip repair
Outline the chronological multidisciplinary surgical roadmap from birth to adolescence (lip at 3 months, palate at 9-12 months, alveolar bone graft at 9 years, orthognathic surgery at maturity)
Educate parents on immediate practical feeding adaptations using specialized positive-pressure cleft bottles to prevent failure to thrive and nasal regurgitation

Syndromic cleft (e.g. Van der Woude syndrome)

must_ask.say: Is your baby having trouble feeding, or does milk come out of the nose?

history.answer: Our two-week-old baby was born with a gap in his upper lip and the roof of his mouth, and we are here for his cleft evaluation.
He was born with this cleft two weeks ago; it was visible right at delivery.
The gap is on the left side of his upper lip and goes up into his left nostril, and the roof of his mouth is completely open inside.
His lip is completely separated all the way into his nose, and the left side of his nose looks flattened and wider.
The cleft itself has stayed the same since birth, but feeding has remained a daily struggle for us.
He cannot form a tight seal to suck on a regular nipple, so he swallows a lot of air and tires out quickly.
Yes, almost every time he drinks formula, milk leaks out through his left nostril.
Holding him in an upright position helps milk go down better, whereas lying him flat makes the choking and nasal regurgitation much worse.
He coughs and splutters when the milk flows too quickly, but he has never turned blue or stopped breathing.
He weighed 3.4 kilograms when he was born, but at his two-week check he was down to 3.3 kilograms, so he hasn't regained his birth weight.
No, he has not had any fever, chills, or warmth.
He produces about five wet diapers each day, though his stools have been somewhat small.
We have been using standard infant bottles and trying to feed him very slowly, but each feeding takes nearly an hour.
He was examined by the pediatric team at the delivery hospital, and they referred us directly to this cleft team for specialized care.
I had regular prenatal checkups and ultrasounds, though the cleft was only clearly confirmed right after delivery.
I took prenatal multivitamins and folic acid daily, and I did not smoke, drink alcohol, or take any prescription medications during pregnancy.
No, his hearing screening in the newborn nursery was normal, and doctors did not find any defects in his heart, kidneys, or limbs.
No, neither of his lips has any small pits, bumps, or fluid-leaking dimples.
We are feeling heartbroken and completely overwhelmed seeing his cleft and worrying about how many operations he will have to go through.
We are terrified that he isn't getting enough nutrition because so much milk comes out of his nose instead of his belly.
We hope you can teach us how to feed him safely today and explain what surgeries he will need and when they should happen.
He has had no other medical conditions or diagnoses since birth.
He has not had any surgical procedures or previous hospital admissions aside from his birth stay.
He does not take any medications, drops, or herbal remedies.
He has no known allergies to medications or latex.
He was born at 39 weeks by an uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery, crying right away with a birth weight of 3.4 kilograms.
He received his newborn vitamin K injection and hepatitis B vaccine before leaving the nursery.
No one in either of our families has ever had a cleft lip, cleft palate, or any other facial difference.
We live together in an apartment; my husband works in an office and I am currently home on maternity leave caring for the baby.
Neither of us smokes, and our home is completely smoke-free.
Neither of us drinks alcohol around our baby.
He stays home with us and has not been exposed to any sick individuals or crowds.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 74/48 mmHg, heart rate 140 beats per minute, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 36.8°C.
Alert and active newborn male in no acute respiratory distress, with visible left facial clefting and no syndromic dysmorphic facies.

Complete left-sided cleft lip disrupting the vermilion, white roll, and Cupid's bow extending into the left nostril floor with alar flattening, and a wide cleft through the alveolus, hard palate, and soft palate uvula.
Both external ears are normally formed without preauricular pits, and both tympanic membranes are clear without acute inflammation.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with good air exchange and no crackles, wheezing, or signs of aspiration.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2, and no heart murmur or gallop appreciated.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender with no palpable masses or organomegaly.
Normal skin turgor and capillary refill under two seconds, with no lower lip pits, fistulas, or birthmarks.
Current weight is 3.3 kg, representing a 100-gram loss from birth weight of 3.4 kg, with normal length and head circumference.
